lit.\u0027\u003cb\u003eM⁺•\u003c/b\u003e = m: "M⁺• = molar mass; odd M ⇒ odd N."
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEl \u003cb\u003edespl:
"

The chemical shift δ (ppm, relative to TMS) depends on the electronic environment: electronegative atoms and carbonyls deshield the carbon. Approximately: alkyl 5–45 · C–N 30–60 · C–O 50–90 · C=C/aromatic 100–150 · acid/ester C=O 160–185 · aldehyde/ketone C=O 190–220 ppm. The signal at ≈ 209 ppm in butanone identifies a ketone carbonyl.

"
"

M⁺• fragments. In ketones, amines and alcohols α-cleavage dominates (the C–C bond next to the heteroatom): propanone → CH₃C≡O⁺ (m/z 43); diethylamine → m/z 58; ethanol → CH₂=OH⁺ (m/z 31). If there is an H at γ to the C=O, the McLafferty rearrangement occurs (pentan-2-one → m/z 58, with loss of ethene). The highlighted fragments are shown on the molecule.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEn \u003cb\u003eespec:
"

In mass spectrometry (electron impact) the molecule loses an electron and forms the molecular ion M⁺•, whose m/z ratio is the molar mass (with z = 1). Ions are separated by m/z and their relative abundance is recorded; the most intense peak is the base peak (100 %). Nitrogen rule: odd M ⇔ odd number of N atoms (diethylamine, M = 73). Unstable ions give lighter fragments.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEn \u003cb\u003eRMN d:
"

In ¹³C NMR (proton-decoupled) each non-equivalent carbon gives one signal. Symmetry reduces the number: propanone (two equivalent CH₃) gives 2 signals; pentan-3-one, 3; butanone, 4 and pentan-2-one, 5. The colors on the molecule show equivalent carbons (same color). Intensity is not proportional to the number of C.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEstrategia: 1) \u003c:
"

Strategy: 1) M and the N rule → formula; 2) isotopes (Cl/Br); 3) characteristic fragments (43 = CH₃CO, 57 = C₂H₅CO, 58 = McLafferty/amine α); 4) no. of ¹³C signals and their δ → functional groups and symmetry. In “Lab” turn on “Problem mode” to hide the name and deduce the structure from the spectra alone.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eLos halógenos tienen:
"

Halogens have very characteristic natural isotopes: ³⁵Cl : ³⁷Cl = 75.8 : 24.2 ≈ 3 : 1; ⁷⁹Br : ⁸¹Br = 50.7 : 49.3 ≈ 1 : 1. A compound with one Cl shows M and M+2 peaks in a 3:1 ratio; with one Br, 1:1. In addition, ¹³C (1.1 %) produces a small M+1 peak ≈ 1.1 % per C, useful for counting carbons.

"
